newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission sets environmental accord framework.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission sets environmental accord framework.

text.p: The European Commission adopted on Wednesday a framework for agreeing environmental accords with polluting industries, raising the prospect of EU-wide charging or taxation regimes intended to cut damage to the environment.
"Promoting such agreements is part of (EU) efforts to complement environmental legislation by market-based instruments," the Commission said in a news statement.
European Environment Commissioner Ritt Bjerregaard said she intended the framework to provide "effective and reliable agreements between public authorities and industry".
Sweden, Finland and Bjerregaard's native Denmark have often used industry agreements instead of binding laws to reduce a variety of pollutants such as sulphur and benzene in fuel.
The Commission has hit on using similar accords as alternatives to binding EU laws, which can take years to adopt.

"Environmental agreements have the advantage that they can promote a proactive attitude on the part of industry, cost-effective and tailor-made solutions and a quicker attainment of goals," the statement said.

Commission guidelines for accords say there should be prior consultation with interested parties and that they should be contractual with quantified objectives, intermediate goals to monitor progress and with independent auditing.

Such accords, by tying industry into specific goals, might also spare the Commission its annual embarrassment as the EU's law enforcer. Last month, the EU executive reported 265 suspected breaches of environmental law chalked up by member states in 1995, with 20 legal texts not written into national law in some countries.

Accords might also offer the Commission an alternative route for EU-level environmental charges or levies, which it has been unable to pursue before because of the need for unanimous approval for any EU tax, which some states oppose in principle.

Such opposition doomed the Commission's proposed carbon tax on fossil fuels, launched to tackle climate-warming carbon dioxide emissions but attacked as damaging to industrial competitiveness and liable to hijack by national treasuries.
